name: Existentialism
kicker: Philosophical movement · Freedom, the absurd, and living authentically
briefing: Imagine being handed a life with no instructions and no built-in purpose — now what? That is the question existentialism tackles, through thinkers like Søren Kierkegaard, Jean-Paul Sartre, and Albert Camus. They argued that people are radically free, fully responsible for their own choices, and must create their own meaning in a universe that offers none on its own.

qb.tip: Only 2 Middle School/Easy High School tossups; a Regular HS search found 2 more that were clearly on-topic, all naming Kierkegaard, Sartre, or Camus.

sample.note: 4 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 2 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: One proponent of this movement, Martin Buber, argued that human life is centered on genuine relationships in his book _I and Thou_. Another figure in this tradition published _Either/Or_ under pseudonyms such as “Judge William” before describing “the dizziness of freedom” in _The Concept of Anxiety_.
tossups.r: Jean-Paul Sartre, the author of _Being and Nothingness_, described giving up one’s own freedom of choice as “bad faith.” For 10 points, name this philosophical movement associated with Søren Kierkegaard and Sartre.

tossups.p: Christian thinkers Nikolai Berdyaev and Paul Tillich both worked within this school of thought. Albert Camus, the author of _A Happy Death_, publicly denied belonging to this movement even though he is still closely linked to it. Søren Kierkegaard described the self as “a relation that relates itself to itself” in _The Sickness Unto Death_.
tossups.r: A central slogan of this movement holds that “existence precedes essence.” For 10 points, name this philosophical movement also associated with Jean-Paul Sartre.

tossups.p: Fyodor Dostoevsky’s _Notes from Underground_ is sometimes read as an early literary forerunner of this movement. Søren Kierkegaard’s _Fear and Trembling_ examines Abraham’s willingness to sacrifice Isaac as an example of a “leap of faith.” Albert Camus ended an essay in this tradition by writing that “one must imagine Sisyphus happy.”
tossups.r: This philosophy centers on the angst, or anxiety, that comes from living in a universe with no built-in meaning. For 10 points, name this movement also associated with Jean-Paul Sartre.

tossups.p: Martin Heidegger’s _Being and Time_ is often linked to this movement, even though Heidegger himself rejected the label. Jean-Paul Sartre argued that people are “condemned to be free,” meaning they cannot escape making choices and owning the results.
tossups.r: This philosophy prizes authenticity, or living true to one’s own values instead of just following the crowd. For 10 points, name this movement that holds people are radically free and fully responsible for their choices, associated with Sartre and Søren Kierkegaard.

tossups.p: Simone de Beauvoir applied ideas from this movement to feminism in her book _The Second Sex_. Søren Kierkegaard, often called the founder of this movement, wrote against Hegel’s abstract philosophical systems. Jean-Paul Sartre defended this movement in a 1945 lecture, later published as an essay arguing that it “is a Humanism.”
tossups.r: A central slogan of this movement holds that “existence precedes essence,” meaning people are not born with a fixed purpose. For 10 points, name this movement associated with Sartre and Kierkegaard.

tossups.p: Jean-Paul Sartre’s play _No Exit_ claims that “Hell is other people,” while Søren Kierkegaard’s _The Sickness Unto Death_ examines despair as a sickness of the self. Sartre also described a person who denies their own freedom of choice as living in “bad faith.”
tossups.r: This philosophy’s key thinkers include Kierkegaard and Sartre, and it centers on the angst of living in a world with no built-in meaning. For 10 points, name this philosophical movement.

tossups.p: Jean-Paul Sartre’s major philosophical treatise, _Being and Nothingness_, examines human consciousness and freedom in great detail. Albert Camus, who wrote that “one must imagine Sisyphus happy” in _The Myth of Sisyphus_, publicly denied belonging to this movement.
tossups.r: Camus is nonetheless closely tied to this school of thought through his idea of the absurd. For 10 points, name this movement also associated with Jean-Paul Sartre.

tossups.p: Martin Buber explored relationships between people and between people and God in _I and Thou_, a work linked to this movement. Søren Kierkegaard’s _Fear and Trembling_ uses the biblical story of Abraham and Isaac to explore faith as a leap beyond reason.
tossups.r: A famous slogan of this movement claims that “existence precedes essence.” For 10 points, name this movement whose key thinkers include Kierkegaard and Jean-Paul Sartre.

tossups.p: Nikolai Berdyaev and Paul Tillich developed a specifically Christian version of this movement. Fyodor Dostoevsky’s novella _Notes from Underground_ is often cited as an early forerunner of its ideas about an isolated, struggling individual.
tossups.r: This philosophy stresses authenticity, radical freedom, and full responsibility for one’s own choices. For 10 points, name this movement associated with Albert Camus and Jean-Paul Sartre.

tossups.p: Martin Heidegger’s _Being and Time_ is often grouped with this movement, although Heidegger rejected that label for himself. Jean-Paul Sartre claimed that people are “condemned to be free” and dramatized the torment of being watched by others in his play _No Exit_.
tossups.r: This philosophy centers on the angst of living in a universe that offers no built-in meaning. For 10 points, name this philosophical movement also linked to Søren Kierkegaard.

tossups.p: Simone de Beauvoir drew on this movement’s ideas about freedom to write _The Second Sex_. Søren Kierkegaard described despair as a “sickness unto death” in a book of that name, exploring how the self relates to itself.
tossups.r: Albert Camus, often grouped with this movement, explored the absurd, the clash between humans’ need for meaning and a silent universe. For 10 points, name this movement whose slogan is “existence precedes essence,” associated with Jean-Paul Sartre.

tossups.p: Jean-Paul Sartre defended this movement in a 1945 lecture, published as an essay arguing that it “is a Humanism.” Søren Kierkegaard wrote under pseudonyms such as “Judge William” in his book _Either/Or_.
tossups.r: Sartre described denying one’s own freedom of choice as living in “bad faith.” For 10 points, name this movement whose major thinkers include Kierkegaard and Sartre.

tossups.p: Fyodor Dostoevsky’s alienated narrator in _Notes from Underground_ is often read as a forerunner of this movement’s ideas. Christian versions of this movement were developed by Nikolai Berdyaev and Paul Tillich.
tossups.r: Albert Camus, who wrote “one must imagine Sisyphus happy” in _The Myth of Sisyphus_, is linked to this movement’s focus on living with the angst of a meaningless universe. For 10 points, name this philosophical movement also tied to Jean-Paul Sartre.

tossups.p: Søren Kierkegaard’s _Fear and Trembling_ uses Abraham’s binding of Isaac to explore a terrifying “leap of faith.” Martin Buber’s _I and Thou_ is sometimes grouped with this movement for its focus on real relationships between people.
tossups.r: This philosophy teaches that people are radically free, fully responsible for their choices, and should live with authenticity. For 10 points, name this movement associated with Kierkegaard and Jean-Paul Sartre.

tossups.p: In Jean-Paul Sartre’s play _No Exit_, a character famously declares that “Hell is other people,” a dramatic example of ideas Sartre laid out in his treatise _Being and Nothingness_. A slogan often used to summarize this movement is “existence precedes essence.”
tossups.r: Albert Camus is closely tied to this movement despite personally rejecting the label. For 10 points, name this philosophical movement whose other key thinkers include Søren Kierkegaard.

trap.title: Movement or one thinker?
trap.body: Quiz bowl sometimes asks for this whole movement, and sometimes asks for one of the individual people in it — Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, and Søren Kierkegaard each have their own separate answer lines. A tossup that strings together clues from several different thinkers, or says “this movement” or “this school of thought,” wants the movement itself, not any one person.
trap.fix: Listen for the wording: “this philosophical movement” or “this school of thought” means the whole tradition. Clues about one person’s specific birthplace, personal life, or entire body of work by themselves usually mean that one philosopher instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Existentialism (accept word forms like existentialist)
